positions.commentary: The speaker indicates META is showing strong momentum with accelerating revenue growth for the third consecutive quarter.
The speaker views Constellation Software favorably, noting its low valuation relative to its significant growth in free cash flow.

thesis: The episode argues that META is the primary beneficiary of AI, showing strong revenue momentum, though its high capital expenditures on data centers and chips create a significant temporary headwind to earnings and free cash flow. In contrast, Louis Vuitton and LVMH are viewed as durable businesses with low AI risk and attractive valuations, while Constellation Software is favored for its low valuation relative to its significant free cash flow growth.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Louis Vuitton is not an AI risk and represents a durable business.
claims.quote: Plus the fact that these do tend to be pretty durable businesses, definitely not an AI risk in Louis Vuitton and Tiffany.

claims.claim: The speaker highlights strong AI-driven growth and revenue increases but warns that high CapEx is creating a significant headwind to earnings and free cash flow conversion.
claims.quote: And it's been phenomenal for them. There's all sorts of different things they called out on the call. Watchtime on Instagram, Reels is up 30% year-to-year in the United States.

claims.claim: Despite growth, the speaker warns that high CapEx spending means reported earnings are not fully reflective of underlying owner earnings due to a headwind.
claims.quote: So if you think that's a normalized earnings figure, you're going to be wrong and you're going to be surprised when there's this big headwind to it.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that free cash flow conversion has dropped significantly in 2025 compared to historical levels due to increased CapEx.
claims.quote: Last time people really were freaking out about Meta was at the time in 2022 if you remember and people may be are forgetting this, revenues were contracting, earnings were not looking good.

claims.claim: The speaker suggests that Meta is the biggest beneficiary of AI, turning advancements into actual revenue growth.
claims.quote: And I think they're going to continue to grow because almost more so than any other business, they seem to be the biggest beneficiary of AI today and actually turning a lot of these advancements into actual revenue growth.

claims.claim: The core business is performing exceptionally well, supported by significant AI-driven growth in watchtime, ad optimization, and conversion, despite high capital expenditures.
claims.quote: Everything is going really, really well for them. They maybe are making some questionable capital allocation decisions. We won't know until after the fact. But the core business is doing really well and kind of supports a lot of these activities too.

claims.claim: META is a major beneficiary of AI, turning advancements into revenue growth, with specific metrics showing significant lifts in watchtime, feed engagement, and ad performance.
claims.quote: Now they're offsetting that by growing a lot, and I think they're going to continue to grow because almost more so than any other business, they seem to be the biggest beneficiary of AI today and actually turning a lot of these advancements into actual revenue growth. And it's been phenomenal for them.

claims.claim: META's top line is growing at over 20 percent, and adjusting for Reality Labs losses brings the valuation multiple closer to 23 times.
claims.quote: If you're pulling out the reality labs losses, then you're getting closer to a 23 times multiple for a company that is growing top line, you know, 20 percent plus.

claims.claim: The speaker questions whether META needed to spend $72 billion in CAPEX last year to achieve its results, suggesting they might have done it with $40 billion.
claims.quote: Now, again, the question is did they need to spend the 72 billion in CAPEX last year to get these results? Could they have done it with 40 maybe? And I'm not saying they shouldn't have spent the 72 to continue to grow.

claims.claim: META's CAPEX is increasing next year to between $115 and $135 billion, which will result in no free cash flow or stock buybacks.
claims.quote: And on the topic of CAPEX, it's going up again next year to $115 to $135 billion. And so there won't be free cash flow next year or stock buybacks.

claims.claim: META has spent over $100 billion on the Reality Labs project, which is now a small fraction of their total CAPEX spending.
claims.quote: And now that's just, you know, dropping the bucket relative to how much they're spending on CAPEX. So that is kind of the big overview there with what's going on in the business.

claims.claim: META's Reality Labs losses are expected to peak next year and then start to decrease thereafter.
claims.quote: They started to say that next year will be the last year of kind of peak losses. And then they'll start to go down thereafter.

claims.claim: META's current valuation is around $1.8 trillion based on a $690 stock price and trailing earnings multiple of about 29 times.
claims.quote: And so, you know, at this $690 stock price right now, you know, you're looking around 1.8 trillion valuation. So on TTM, they are in 2350 last year trailing for about a 29 times multiple.

claims.claim: META's high CAPEX spending on data centers and chips creates a temporary earnings headwind due to depreciation not fully accounting for the capital intensity.
claims.quote: And then one last comment because sometimes people comment on this because I always use trailing multiples and trailing earnings instead of forward. And I have a very good reason for this, in my opinion, which is that it doesn't really make sense to me for you to mix future forward earnings with a multiple, which is essentially a shorthand for a DCF.

claims.claim: The speaker views Constellation Software favorably, noting its low valuation relative to its significant growth in free cash flow.
claims.quote: But right now, as we speak, Constellation, you know, the US ticker, CNSFW, is trading at around 17 times free cash flow. And so it's interesting because it's not quite, but almost back to the spot where it was at when we originally wrote about it three years ago. And free cash flow has actually grown over 150% since then.

claims.claim: The speaker highlights that LVMH's core brands are not exposed to AI risks and suggests the stock is undervalued relative to normalized earnings multiples.
claims.quote: Plus the fact that these do tend to be pretty durable businesses, definitely not an AI risk in Louis Vuitton and Tiffany.
